Q: How do we check container logs in kubernetes before they are written to the log file? A:

As stated above, all log output should be written directly to stdout, so that k8s can store it in the filesystem of the node and/or forward it to a central sink like ELK, depending on your setup.

If you suspect there's something going wrong or the app writes to a logfile inside the container, then you could give liblogtap a try which is designed be be injected into the container without having to mofdify the original image. You'd need to add an init container to inject the library and a sidecar to pick up (and maybe forward) the logs.

Q: "addLast" method in a doubly linked only works once on an empty list, and not at all otherwise A:

There are several problems.

First, your doubly linked list's addLast method doesn't set the next attribute of the tail node to point to the newly created node. It only sets a prev attribute, never a next.

You might have missed this thinking the inheritance would take care of this, but the append nor add method of the base class LinkedList are ever called.

Secondly, if you would have called the base class method, there would still be a problem, because the append method does not update the value of self.tail, so that self.tail is not guaranteed to point to the tail node.

I suppose you intended the LinkedList code to take care of the next attributes, and the DoublyLinkedList code of the prev attributes. So then you first need to correct the bug in the append method. For instance, like this:

    def append(self, value):
        if self.count == 0:
            return self.add(value)
        # by definition the tail has its next attribute set to None (no loop needed)
        self.tail.next = Node(value)
        self.tail = self.tail.next  # update the reference to the tail
        self.count += 1

In the DoublyLinkedList class, rely on the above code by calling it from the addLast method. It could be like this:

    def addLast(self, item):
        prev_tail = self.tail
        super().append(item)        # apply the logic from base class
        if prev_tail:
            self.tail.prev = prev_tail

Your addFirst has a similar problem, as it only sets the next attributes, not the prev attributes. You don't notice this with turning the list to a string -- as that only relies on the next attributes -- but the prev attributes will not be correctly set. Here is a possibly way to correc that:

    def addFirst(self, item):
        super().add(item)           # apply the logic from base class
        if self.head.next:
            self.head.next.prev = self.head

Q: The pointer existential crisis dilemma: If pointer stores memory address then how are memory addresses of a pointers stored? A:

Pointers are objects as any other objects of other types. You may take an address of any object that is not a temporary object or is not declared with storage class specifier register.

Consider the following declaration

T x;

where T is a type.

When you can declare a pointer that points to this variable

T *p = &x;

Now you can define the type T as for example

typedef int *T;

In this case the type of the pointer p will be T *. That is for the variable p the program allocates memory of the size sizeof( p ) and stores there the value of the address of the variable x.

The type T can be defined in turn as a pointer type as for example

typedef int ***T;

In this case the variable x itself will have the pointer type int *** and the variable p will have a pointer to pointer type that is int ****. The memory for pointers are allocated the same way as for other scalar types.

Q: Get row index ranges by grouped name, preserving order and gaps A:

Using index - ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY name ORDER BY index) to generate additional continuous group:

with src AS (
SELECT *, index - ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY name ORDER BY index) AS grp
FROM unnest(ARRAY[
    NULL, NULL,
    'foo', 'foo', 'foo',
    NULL, NULL, NULL,
    'bar', 'bar',
    NULL,
    'foo', 'foo'
]) WITH ORDINALITY _(name, index)
)
SELECT name, MIN(index) || '-' || MAX(index) AS range
FROM src
GROUP BY name, grp
ORDER BY MIN(index);

Output:

name    range
null    1-2
foo     3-5
null    6-8
bar     9-10
null    11-11
foo     12-13
